name: Xhosa
confidence_why: McLaren 1906, Downing 1990 (following Doke 1954), Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1997 and Gowlett 2003 all put Xhosa's regular prominence, realised as lengthening, on the penult, and Jokweni 1995 confirms the long penult while treating it as a phrase-final process rather than word stress; only Jordan 1956 dissents, denying fixed penultimate stress and placing emphatic stress on the root syllable, but he concedes that stress is seldom prominent in ordinary speech and no later source adopts his view.

catalog_locator: Sec. 8 'Accentuation', pp. 11-12; and sec. 2 'Vowel Sounds', p. 2 ('In general, accented syllables are long, and unaccented syllables are short').
catalog_quote: As a general rule, the accent in Kaffir is put upon the penult, that is, the last syllable but one, as bámba, ubúso, andibóni. When a word is lengthened by inflexion at the end, the accent is moved forward so as to remain on the penult, as bambáni, ebuswéni, andibonánga. When a monosyllabic word or particle is closely joined to a preceding word, it draws forward the accent in the same way, as hambá-ke, andiboní-na, umniní-mzi, ndawó-nye. ... To the general rule there are several exceptions. The accent is on the last syllable :— (a) In the case of several nouns with monosyllabic roots, especially nouns with the prefix ili, pl. ama, as ili-zwí, ama-té, ama-só. (b) In the case of some verbs with monosyllabic roots, as ndiká, I draw (water); yitá, pour out. (c) In the short form of the perfect tense of verbs, as bafiké izolo, they arrived yesterday. ... [p. 12] The principal accent is on the first syllable :— (a) In the past indefinite tense of the indicative mood, as sákangela, sáteta. (b) In adverbs compounded with the prefix pa, pe, as pákati, pámbili, pézulu. Long derivative words have a secondary accent on the syllable which would be the penult in the simple word from which they are derived, as umtételéli from teta, uménzeleléli from énza.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Xhosa is not in the catalog. Six title-keyword items: two were read. (1) Goldsmith, Peterson & Drogo 1989 was downloaded from Goldsmith's UChicago page (scan, scanned) - it is about metrical 'accent' as a tone-attraction target (antepenult by default, H-toned penult, final vowel extrametrical in the present indicative), not phonetic stress; its note says it revises Peterson 1985, so that print-only working paper is covered. (2) Downing 1990 (already held by the project under nort2795, copied here) gives the only first-hand stress statement in the set: the Nguni penult (Zulu, Xhosa, Ndebele) 'is lengthened.. due to regular stress on that syllable' (p. 310; p. 304 'stress-induced lengthening of the penult'), with the antepenult accent kept separate. Not obtainable: Roux 1995 (SAJAL, doi 10.1080/02572117.1995.10587055, paywalled, content unclear from title), Mosaka 2000 (SAJAL, doi 10.1080/02572117.2000.10587424, paywalled - the top acquisition target, the only item whose title is squarely stress assignment in Xhosa), Downing 2003 (FAB 15, print only; cited second-hand in Bloom Ström 2022 for H on penult/antepenult; Downing 2004 ZASPiL held by the project covers the same ground). Side find: 'Xhosa: A tone or pitch accent language?' SAJL 1998, doi 10.1080/10118063.1998.9724401 (not in the item list, closed).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary accent on the penultimate syllable of the word, recomputed over word + monosyllabic enclitic (-ke, -na, -nye, etc.) so that it stays penultimate in the enlarged unit; accented syllables are long (p. 6). Modern phonological work (Jokweni 1994/1995, Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1998, Zerbian 2004, Bloom Ström 2022) describes the same prominence as automatic penultimate vowel lengthening, strongest on the penult of a phonological-phrase/utterance-final word, with lexical H tones independently targeting the antepenult or penult; Xhosa has no lexical vowel-length contrast and is a two-tone language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: McLaren p. 12: long derivative words carry a secondary accent on the syllable that would be the penult of the simple base (umtételéli < teta, uménzeleléli < énza); compounds carry a secondary accent on the penult of the first member (umtételiwáka, hlángabéza). Appleyard 1850 sec. 66 similarly notes a lighter 'fore-tone' on prefixes of words of three or more syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: McLaren pp. 11-12: final accent in (a) some monosyllabic-root nouns esp. with ili-/ama- (ili-zwí, ama-té, ama-só), (b) some monosyllabic-root verbs (ndiká, yitá), (c) the short perfect (bafiké izolo), (d) calling at a distance (nxámá wetú), (e) demonstratives/adverbs in -a (eliyá, payá); initial accent in the past indefinite (sákangela, sáteta) and adverbs with pa-/pe- (pákati, pámbili, pézulu); ideophones with ukuti keep their own accent (ndáti-nqá). Modern sources: penultimate lengthening is reduced/suspended in polar and content questions and fast speech (Jones 2001, Bloom Ström 2022) and absent on phrase-medial words (Cassimjee & Kisseberth p. 54; Jokweni).
new_statements.domain_note: McLaren states the rule for the word (citation forms) and word+enclitic group. Modern instrumental and phonological work locates the main lengthening at the right edge of the phonological phrase/utterance (Jokweni 1995 via Zerbian 2004; Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1998 p. 51 'automatic lengthening that affects the penultimate syllable of a word that stands in utterance-final position'); Bloom Ström 2022 p. 87 reports a three-way gradient non-penult < word-penult (half-long, 100-200 ms) < utterance-penult (>200 ms, mean 217 ms in declaratives). Xhosa is tonal (H vs toneless), no lexical length; 'stress' here = penultimate length prominence, independent of H-tone placement (antepenult/penult).
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe standard/literary Xhosa (xhos1239, ISO xho); McLaren 1906 and Appleyard 1850 call it 'Kaffir/Kafir', the colonial-era name for Xhosa (McLaren's book was retitled 'A Xhosa Grammar' from 1936). No dialect restriction stated (Mpondo, Bhaca etc. not separately treated).

new_statements.reading: Xhosa, as a Nguni language (the paper's Xhosa data come from Claughton 1983 and Westphal & Notschweleka 1967), has regular penultimate stress, phonetically realised as lengthening of the penult, most clearly at the end of a phrase. The antepenult 'accent' of the Goldsmith-Peterson-Drogo/Downing tone-shift analyses is an abstract metrical device that attracts H tone and is explicitly distinct from this penult stress. Caveat held by the project from the earlier check: Jordan 1956 (UCT PhD, vol. 1 secs. 2.113-2.126) argues that the Bantuist 'penultimate main stress' view confuses length with stress and that emphatic stress falls on the root syllable; a coder should weigh a first-hand length-based penult statement (Downing, Doke) against Jordan's dissent.

new_statements.quote: In general, IsiXhosa does not have a vowel length contrast between words. new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penult record and with McLaren 1906 and Downing 1990: the prominent (long) syllable is the penult, and it shifts to the new penult under suffixation. It adds the domain: lengthening is bounded by the Phonological Phrase (right edge), so a word only shows it phrase-finally or in isolation, and it is a post-lexical process, not a lexical length or stress property. It does not itself call the penult prominence 'stress' (unlike Downing 1990 p. 310), and its antepenult 'metrical prominence' is a tone-shift device, not stress; so it neither confirms nor denies Jordan 1956's dissent that root-syllable emphasis, not the penult, is stress proper.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dissertation never makes a word-stress claim for Xhosa: the word 'stress' occurs once, in a general definition of focus ('a focused word is the one which bears the accent or the primary stress', p. 30, citing Chomsky, Jackendoff, Selkirk, Rochemont), and 'accent' only in that line and in bibliography titles. What it does state is that the long penultimate vowel is not lexical but the output of a post-lexical domain-limit rule, Penultimate Vowel Lengthening, applying at the right edge of the Phonological Phrase (a word in isolation is its own Phonological/Intonational Phrase, so citation forms lengthen the penult: /intaka/ -> (intaaka) 'bird', (intakaana) 'small bird', *(intaakana), p. 26); phrase-medial words do not lengthen ('Phonological Phrase-medially Penultimate Vowel Lengthening does not apply', p. 176). It also reports, from Goldsmith/Peterson/Drogo and Downing, the metrical device that puts abstract prominence on the antepenult to attract the rightmost H tone (p. 11), and quotes Ziervogel 1967 for three length grades: long penult in isolation or phrase/sentence-finally, half-long penult phrase-internally, short in some ideophones, monosyllabic demonstratives and at the end of an interrogative clause (p. 9).
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate lengthening is absent phrase-medially (p. 176) and, per the Ziervogel quotation on p. 9, in certain ideophones, monosyllabic demonstratives and at the end of an interrogative clause; the derived diminutive shows the length moving to the new penult (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: Jokweni 1995 describes IsiXhosa generally (standard/written Xhosa is said to originate from the IsiRharhabe dialect, p. 5-6); data are the author's own intuitions plus two native speakers in the US (Zimbini Qaba, Nombuyiselo Lupiwana) and the larger corpus compiled by F. Cassimjee and verified by Xhosa speakers at Illinois (sec. 1.6.1, printed p. 19). No dialect is assigned to the data.

readall_conflicts: No new contradiction. Jokweni 1995 takes no position on word stress; it describes the penult prominence as post-lexical Penultimate Vowel Lengthening at the right edge of the Phonological Phrase, which is compatible with the catalog's penultimate record and with McLaren 1906 (penult accent, moving with suffixation) and Downing 1990 (penult lengthened 'due to regular stress on that syllable'). The pre-existing disagreement stands: Jordan 1956 (UCT PhD, vol. 1 secs. 2.119-2.126) holds that the Bantuist 'penultimate main stress' view confuses length with stress and that emphatic stress falls on the root syllable; Jokweni's phrase-level account of the length is neutral on that question. The antepenultimate 'metrical prominence' Jokweni reports from Goldsmith, Peterson & Drogo and Downing is an abstract H-tone attractor, not stress, and should not be read as an antepenult stress claim.
